references.text: Your descendants shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south. In you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.
I will bless you abundantly and make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as the sand on the seashore. Your offspring shall possess the gates of their enemies.
I will make your descendants like the dust of the earth. If anyone can count the dust of the earth, then your descendants may also be counted.

Now the Scriptures say that the promises were given to Abraham and his offspring. It does not say: "and to offsprings", as if it referred to many, but rather as if it referred to one: "and to your offspring", and this is Christ.
Jacob quotes directly from the promise in 16:10 that the descendants will be so numerous they cannot be counted.
Both verses confirm God's promise to make Abraham's descendants a multitude of nations, even though the metaphor varies.
Isaiah uses the same sand metaphor as a contrasting image of what would have happened to Israel's descendants if they had been obedient.
New Testament confirmation of the same covenant promise of endless blessing and numerousness that Jacob quotes.
Prophetic application of Abraham's 'sand' metaphor to David's descendants, showing the continuity of God's promise.
Prophetic reuse of Abraham's promise about the 'sand of the sea' which cannot be counted, to describe God's restoration of Israel.
